# Advising a Peruvian Municipal Utility on NRW Reduction (42% NRW, PEN 2M, 60,000 pop.)

## First: Don't spend the money yet

A board that says "fix leakage" with 42% NRW and no diagnostic breakdown is about to spend PEN 2 million on guesswork. The single highest-value intervention available is a **IWA/World Bank standard water balance and DMA-level audit**, and it should consume real budget before pipes get touched.

## What the split is likely to be, and why it matters

For a mid-size Peruvian utility (EPS-scale, typically similar profile to Sunass-regulated companies outside Lima), with 42% NRW, a reasonable prior — before you have data — is:

| Component | Typical share of NRW | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical losses** (real leakage — mains, connections, service lines, storage overflow) | ~55–65% | Aging asbestos-cement/PVC networks, high pressure zones, poor repair quality are endemic in Peruvian secondary cities |
| **Commercial losses** (illegal connections, meter under-registration, billing/data errors) | ~35–45% | Meter parks are often old (many EPS have >10yr average meter age), micro-metering coverage is incomplete, and clandestine connections are common in peri-urban expansion areas |

**Why this matters financially, not just technically:** physical losses cost you *production* money (chemicals, energy, water rights fees) but commercial losses cost you *revenue* directly — water you already paid to produce and deliver, that nobody pays you for. In many Peruvian EPS, commercial losses are actually the **larger share of the financial loss**, even when physical losses are the larger share of the *volume* lost, because:
- Peru's marginal cost of treatment/pumping per m³ is often lower than the tariff per m³
- Under-registration by old meters commonly runs 15–30% on aging meter parks
- Illegal connections concentrate in exactly the low-income peri-urban zones that grew fastest and were never properly cadastered

So even if physical loss is the bigger *bucket*, commercial loss reduction usually has the faster payback period.

## Recommended allocation of PEN 2,000,000

**1. Water balance audit + DMA design (PEN 150,000–200,000)**
- Full IWA water balance, minimum 3-6 months of bulk metering data
- Establish or confirm District Metered Areas (DMAs) — you cannot manage what you can't isolate and measure
- This tells you your *actual* physical/commercial split, ILI (Infrastructure Leakage Index), and prioritizes zones

**2. Commercial loss reduction (PEN 700,000–900,000) — front-load this**
- Meter replacement program targeting oldest/largest-diameter meters first (they under-register most and serve highest-consumption customers — best ROI)
- Illegal connection cadastre/regularization campaign, ideally combined with an amnesty-to-legalize push rather than pure enforcement
- Billing system audit — check for zero-consumption accounts, estimated bills stuck at old values, commercial/residential misclassification
- This category typically pays for itself within 12–24 months via recovered billed volume

**3. Physical loss reduction (PEN 700,000–900,000) — targeted, not network-wide**
- **Active leak detection** (acoustic loggers, correlators) deployed *within the DMAs identified in step 1* — not blanket pipe replacement
- **Pressure management**: PRVs (pressure reducing valves) in high-pressure zones — often the single best PEN-per-m³-saved intervention in Andean/coastal towns with elevation-driven pressure problems
- Repair of identified bursts/leaks found via the survey — targeted, not speculative digging

**4. Reserve / contingency (PEN 100,000–150,000)**
- Peru's rainy season and informal settlement growth will surface unplanned repairs; don't zero out the buffer

## What to explicitly avoid

- **Blanket pipe replacement** without DMA-level evidence — this is the classic way boards burn budgets on the wrong streets while leakage continues elsewhere
- **Buying leak-detection equipment without training staff to sustain use** — many Peruvian EPS have correlators sitting unused after donor-funded projects ended
- **Ignoring commercial loss because it feels like "not really losing water"** — it's the same lost sol per m³ from the utility's P&L perspective, and Sunass (the regulator) will judge tariff review performance partly on collection efficiency, not just physical loss

## Bottom line for the board

Spend ~10% on finding out where the water and money are actually going, then split the rest roughly 45/45 between metering/commercial fixes (faster payback, addresses revenue directly) and targeted pressure management + leak repair (addresses volume directly) — guided by DMA data, not intuition about which pipes "look old."
